turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): So I booked in because there's this lump on the side of my neck. It's been there three weeks and it doesn't hurt at all, which is the weird part, I keep waiting for it to be sore. I finally stopped poking it and googling pictures at one in the morning and just came in. Sorry, I talk a lot when I'm nervous.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Three weeks and painless, ok. Any fever with it?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no fever. I checked yesterday arvo with the chemist thermometer and it was 36.4, so I don't think I'm running hot.
[SEG0004] person_3 (NURSE): Yep. On our thermometer just now it's 36.6. Pulse is 76, blood pressure 118 over 72.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, close enough to what I got at home. Err, sorry, side note, the renos next door mean I can't hear myself think in the flat, but that's not why I'm here. I just overshare when I'm sitting still.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Which side is the lump, and has it been getting bigger?

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Right side, just under the jaw, sort of where the gland sits. It's about the size of a grape, and I measured it with a bit of string last Tuesday and again this morning and it's the same length, so I don't reckon it's growing. Skin over the top looks normal, not red, not hot. It moves a bit if I push it, which I probably shouldn't keep doing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cuts lately that were slow to heal, or a wound that hung around?
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Oh, can I jump in. The cat got her about a fortnight back. Scratch on the forearm healed in five days, I kept an eye on it.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, she's right. Five days, it went pink and then it was just gone, and I was sure it'd go manky.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Night sweats at all? Waking up drenched?

[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Once. Only the once, I had to get up and change my shirt because it was actually damp, not just warm. I think it was last Thursday, or, umm, it might've been the Thursday before that, I genuinely can't pin the night. Nothing since, I'm not soaking the sheets as a habit.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's your energy? Have you been tired or run down?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Energy's fine. I'm a uni student and I'm still getting to class, I'm not wrecked.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest wise, any cough, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Chest is clear, no cough, and I'm not puffing on the stairs.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking, medicine wise?
[SEG0018] person_3 (NURSE): File says sertralene, 50 mg, once a day.
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Except Sundays. She doesn't take it on Sundays, the Sunday blister stays full.

[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, two corrections if that's ok. They put me up to a hundred milligrams nearly two years ago for the anxiety, so the 50 on the file is the old dose. And it's Saturdays I skip, not Sundays, I forget after footy and I do take the Sunday one. Every other day it's the one tablet.
[SEG0021] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Right. Saturdays, I had the day wrong.

[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so I'm not going to lock a dose in when the file says one thing and you're taking another. Separate question, even if mornings feel ok, do you crash later in the day?

[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah. By the arvo I feel like a wet rag, I crash on the couch and I can't even be bothered making toast, which I didn't want to say because mornings I'm fine. I thought if I can get to uni I'm not tired, but the second half of the day I'm useless. So scrap what I said before.

[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, and some mornings I've got a frog in my throat, the voice comes out all croaky until I've had a tea and then it settles. I've overdone it at training a couple of times lately but that's just footy, not this lump thing.

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me feel. There's a lump on the right under the jaw, about two centimetres, it moves, and it's not tender when I press. Skin over it isn't red. I can't feel any other lumps down the neck or above the collarbone, and the throat looks unremarkable.

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking out loud, a painless node for three weeks plus that cat scratch makes me lean towards a reactive lymph node, possibly cat scratch disease. I'm not calling it that for certain. The one drenching sweat means I also can't properly exclude a lymphoma until the tests are back.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book bloods today, full blood count, CRP and bartonella serology, and an ultrasound of the neck. If the scan looks worrying we might need a needle biopsy, but that's not ordered now. Reception can book the ultrasound on your way out, and we'll do the bloods before you leave.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through it all. If the lump suddenly gets huge, or you spike a proper fever, don't wait for me, come back sooner or go to emergency.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok. Bloods and a scan, and I'll try to remember the Saturday tablet, I know I talk too much. Thanks for not rushing me out.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): You were right to come in. Nurse can take the bloods now, and reception will book the ultrasound on the way out.

spec.situation: Young adult with a painless neck lump for three weeks, night sweats once, no fever now; recent cat scratch mentioned; doctor examines and orders blood tests and ultrasound.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: A caregiver or relative reports observations ('the cut healed in five days', 'she sleeps badly', 'he does not take the tablets on Sundays'); the patient agrees, disagrees or corrects one point. The nurse also reports a measurement that the patient mentioned before.
traps.label_rule: reported_by follows who said it. A healing cut that healed normally is a negative finding (no slow-healing wounds) or nothing, NOT a symptom. A disputed fact is recorded with certainty disputed or as an uncertainty. A correction replaces the earlier value (Saturday, not Sunday).

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Anxiety is stated, but duration refers to dose increase nearly two years ago, not anxiety duration.
Caregiver says scratch healed in five days; temporality is past, not current.
